info.title: Arazzo Workflow Runner API
info.summary: The only path from a runner to durable run state.
info.description:
The surface every runner store interaction goes through (ADR 0065). Before it, a runner held store credentials and claimed, leased, and checkpointed against the store directly; a compromised or curious runner could therefore read and write another tenant's rows, and tenant separation rested on runner-resident code. Here the control plane owns the store exclusively and a runner holds no store credential at all.

It is a **separate document and a separately deployable component** from the governance API, not a section of it. ADR 0023's point survives: execution load never rides the governance request path, and the runner API is scaled and kept available ahead of governance, which is a security-adjacent requirement rather than a capacity preference.

## Authentication

No platform credential is minted for a runner. It authenticates with the machine principal it already has (client credentials, private-key JWT, or mTLS through the deployment's IdP), so decommissioning a host leaves no long-lived platform-issued secret behind. The principal's environment bindings are resolved per request from a bounded cache, which is what gives the runner revocation fence its effect. **Lease ownership derives from the authenticated principal.** A client-supplied owner is rejected rather than trusted, and revocation expires leases by principal, so a compromised runner cannot rename itself into another's leases.

## Refusals

Refusals are non-disclosing. Every operation over a run presents a lease, and an operation naming a run outside the principal's bindings fails that check exactly as one naming a run that does not exist, so this surface cannot be used to enumerate another tenant's runs. Only a capability failure answers `403`. A `404` is reserved for the narrow case of a run the principal does hold whose row is nonetheless absent: there the row was deleted or is being withheld, and the runner faults rather than continuing.

Quota rejections answer `429` and name the quota and its counter, so a runner holds and backs off rather than faulting an advance whose external calls have already landed. That hold is bounded by a total hold time and an attempt cap; past those the advance fails like any other non-2xx, because an unbounded hold would be a silent stall primitive.

## What never appears here

No response body carries key material. A per-lease or per-run key handed back in a claim would put a key that opens every checkpoint of that lease into the hands of the party this design exists to exclude.

servers.description: The runner API host: a separately scalable component sharing the store with the governance API.

tags.name: claims
tags.description: Taking a claimable run and its lease in one operation. The runner never queries the store's dispatch index itself.

tags.name: leases
tags.description: A lease is the run's single-dispatcher interlock. Its owner is the authenticated principal, and its grant carries the server-minted epoch a checkpoint is written under.

tags.name: checkpoints
tags.description: The run row, read and written under a held lease. The checkpoint document is opaque octets to this API: it is carried as a stream rather than embedded in JSON, both because a base64 wrap would inflate the hottest path in the system by a third and because a sealed environment's payload is ciphertext the control plane cannot parse.

post.summary: Claim a run and take its lease
post.description:
Takes the first claimable run the runner can execute and returns it with a fresh lease grant. One operation rather than a query followed by an acquire: the store's dispatch index is not a runner-visible surface, and a two-step form would race between the query and the acquire, wasting lease attempts on runs another runner had already taken.

Claimable means a Pending run, a Running run whose lease has expired (an orphan left by a crashed runner, which must be reclaimable or an interrupted run would never resume), or one marked resume-claimable. The candidate set is intersected server-side with the environments the principal is bound to, so a runner cannot claim a run pinned to an environment it does not serve. The environment is never a request parameter for that reason.

Answers `204` when nothing is claimable, which is the common case for an idle runner and is not an error.

200.description: A run was claimed and its lease granted.

204.description: Nothing is claimable for this runner right now.

post.description:
Extends the lease a runner already holds, so a long advance does not have its run reclaimed as an orphan underneath it. The presented lease token must be the current one; a renewal for a lease that has expired, been released, or been revoked answers `409` rather than silently minting a new one, because the run may already have been claimed by another runner. A run outside the principal's bindings answers the same `409`, so a renewal cannot be used to probe for one.

The epoch does not change on renewal. A new epoch is minted per grant, not per extension, so renewing does not invalidate checkpoints already written under the grant. The token does not change either, so the value already held stays valid for the extended lease.

delete.description:
Hands the run back so another runner may claim it without waiting for the lease to expire. The presented lease is checked before anything is released, because a release matched on the run and the token alone would let one principal release another's lease.

The answer is `204` whether the lease was current, had already lapsed, or was never this principal's. The postcondition the operation promises is that this principal does not hold the run, and that is true in all three cases; distinguishing them would tell a caller about a lease it does not hold.

204.description: The principal does not hold the run.

get.description:
Returns the run's checkpoint document as opaque octets, with the sequence the store has persisted so the runner knows what its next save must propose. Gated on a held lease: reading a run's state is a tenant-data read, so it requires the same interlock as writing it.

The lease check is also the non-disclosure rule here. A run outside the principal's bindings, one held by another runner, and one that does not exist all fail it identically and answer `409`, so this surface cannot be used to learn which of the three it was.

A `404` therefore means something narrower and more serious: the lease is current, and the row is nonetheless absent. A runner holding a non-terminal anchor entry for the run treats that as a fault rather than as a fresh run.

X-Arazzo-Checkpoint-Seq.description: The sequence the store has persisted. The next save must propose exactly this plus one.

put.description:
Replaces the run's single row under compare-and-swap. The runner proposes a sequence and the server accepts **only** the persisted sequence plus one; it validates rather than assigns, so the value is predictable to the writer at the moment it authors the checkpoint and authoritative in the store afterwards.

The store-level compare-and-swap is the etag **and** the persisted sequence together, but the runner supplies only the sequence: the server holds the etag it last wrote and threads it, so a runner carrying one as well would be carrying a second predicate that can never disagree with the first. A save that loses the predicate answers `409` carrying the accepted sequence, and **never** `204`: a superseded save reported as success is indistinguishable from a durable write, which would leave a runner's anchor committed to a checkpoint the store does not have. That is the one failure this operation exists to make impossible.

A retry is a byte-identical resend of the same sequence, not a fresh authoring. The response is `204` rather than the stored document, because the runner already holds the bytes it sent and returning them would double the cost of the hottest operation in the system.

parameters.name: X-Arazzo-Checkpoint-Seq
parameters.description: The proposed sequence. Accepted only when it is exactly the persisted sequence plus one.

X-Arazzo-Checkpoint-Seq.description: The accepted sequence, equal to the proposed one.

post.summary: Claim the runs whose durable timer is now due
post.description:
Takes the suspended runs whose durable timer has fired and returns each with a fresh lease grant, so a runner resumes a waiting run without querying the store's wait index.

As with claiming a new run this is one operation rather than a query followed by an acquire, and for a sharper reason here: the due set is not ordered, so a runner claiming one at a time would keep drawing whichever run the query happened to return first and make no progress through the rest.

The candidate set is intersected server-side with the environments the principal is bound to, and with the runner's hostedVersions, so a runner is never handed a due run it is not authorised for or cannot execute.

post.summary: Claim the runs awaiting a message on a channel
post.description:
Takes the suspended runs awaiting a message on the given channel and correlation id, and returns each with a fresh lease grant. The runner then hands its copy of the message to each run and advances it.

The payload never reaches the control plane. This operation asks which runs a message can resume, not what the message contains, which is why a delivered message is the runner's to hold rather than something it forwards.

A message can resume many runs at once, so the result is a set. The candidate set is intersected server-side with the environments the principal is bound to and with the runner's hostedVersions, so two environments awaiting the same channel name never resume each other's runs.

get.summary: List the versions this runner may execute
get.description:
Answers what this runner should host, resolved from the environments its principal is bound to and what each has made available.

A runner previously read the catalog itself and treated everything in it as hostable, which needed a credential for the whole catalog and gave a runner sight of versions it had no business executing. Being told what to host needs neither.

The set is paged, because a deployment's catalog grows without bound while a runner's poll must not.

parameters.name: pageToken
parameters.description: Opaque continuation token from a previous page.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Page size; the server bounds it.

200.description: The versions this runner may execute.

get.summary: Pull one document of a version's package
get.description:
Serves a named package document (the executor assembly, its manifest, the manifest's detached signature) as opaque octets, so a runner loads an executor without a catalog credential.

Served only for a version available in an environment the principal is bound to. A version the runner may not execute is answered `404` rather than `403`, because saying 'forbidden' would confirm that the version exists.

The bytes are opaque to this operation. Whether the assembly is the right one is settled by the content hash and the manifest signature the runner verifies after pulling, not by having been served from here.

get.summary: Read one version this runner may execute
get.description:
Serves a single version's identity and content hash, for a runner that already knows which version it needs and would otherwise have to page the whole hosted list to find the hash.

The hash is what the loaded executor is verified against, so it has to come from here rather than from the executor's own manifest: a manifest that vouched for itself would prove nothing.

oauth2.description: The machine principal's own token. Client credentials only: there is no interactive flow here, because a runner is never a person. The authorization server is the deployment's, and the URL below is a placeholder.

scopes.runner:execute: Claim runs, hold leases, and load and save checkpoints for the environments this principal is bound to.

openIdConnect.description: OpenID Connect discovery for the same machine principals. The URL below is a placeholder.

mtls.description: Mutual TLS, where the deployment identifies runners by client certificate rather than by bearer token. The certificate subject is the machine principal.

LeaseTokenHeader.name: X-Arazzo-Lease
LeaseTokenHeader.description: The token from the lease grant. Every operation on a run presents it, and the server checks that the lease is current and that its owner is this principal. The owner is never taken from the request.

VersionNumberPath.name: versionNumber
VersionNumberPath.description: The version number within the base workflow.

DocumentNamePath.name: documentName
DocumentNamePath.description: The package document to pull, such as the executor assembly, its manifest, or the manifest's detached signature.

Forbidden.description: The principal lacks the capability. Reserved for capability failures alone: anything out of the principal's environment bindings answers 404 instead, so this response never reveals that a run exists.

NotFound.description: The run is held by this principal and its row is nonetheless absent, so it was deleted or is being withheld. A runner holding a non-terminal anchor entry for the run treats this as a fault rather than a benign miss. A run this principal does not hold never reaches this response: it fails the lease check first and answers 409, which is what keeps a nonexistent run and another tenant's run indistinguishable.

LeaseLost.description: The presented lease is not current. It expired, was released, or was revoked, and the run may already be held by another runner; a run outside this principal's bindings and a run that does not exist answer identically, which is what makes the refusal non-disclosing.

value.title: Lease is no longer held
value.detail: The lease for run 'adopt-42' expired at 2026-08-02T11:04:07Z.

CheckpointWriteRefused.description: The save was not applied, for one of the two reasons a save is refused: the presented lease is not current, or the proposed sequence is not the persisted sequence plus one. The two are told apart by `type`, and the accepted sequence is carried on the second so the runner can tell a duplicate resend from a genuine divergence without a second round trip. Nothing was written either way.

superseded.summary: Another writer advanced the run first

value.title: Checkpoint superseded
value.detail: Sequence 7 was proposed; the store has persisted 7 and accepts 8 next.

PayloadTooLarge.description: The checkpoint exceeds the deployment's body-size cap.

QuotaExceeded.description: A per-tenant quota is exhausted. Retryable, and distinguishable from a fault for exactly that reason: the runner holds and backs off rather than failing an advance whose external calls have already landed. The hold is bounded by a total time and an attempt cap.

checkpointRate.summary: The environment's checkpoint rate is exhausted

value.title: Quota exceeded
value.detail: The checkpoint rate for environment 'production' is exhausted.

RunId.description: A run id. Bounded because it arrives from outside the control plane's boundary and reaches a store key.

LeaseToken.description: The token from a lease grant, opaque to the runner that presents it.

ClaimRequest.description: What the runner can execute. The environment is absent by design: it is resolved from the principal's bindings, because a client-supplied environment would be a request to claim another tenant's work.

hostedVersions.description: The versioned workflow ids ({base}-v{n}) this runner has baked and can execute. A run for a version absent from this list is not offered, since claiming work the runner cannot execute would strand it until the lease expired.

leaseSeconds.description: The requested lease duration. The server bounds it; a request above the deployment's maximum is granted the maximum rather than refused.

ClaimedRun.description: The claimed run and the lease taken over it. It deliberately carries no checkpoint and no key material: the runner loads the checkpoint under the lease it has just been granted, and a key handed back here would open every checkpoint of the lease.

workflowId.description: The versioned workflow id the run executes, from the runner's own hostedVersions.

environment.description: The environment the run is pinned to. Echoed so the runner can select the right credentials and bindings, never taken from the request.

LeaseRenewal.description: An optional renewal request body. Carries no owner: the owner is the authenticated principal.

leaseSeconds.description: The requested extension. The server bounds it as it does at claim.

LeaseGrant.description: A lease over one run. The owner is not a member: it is the authenticated principal, so there is nothing here a compromised runner could rewrite to impersonate another.

token.description: The token to present on every subsequent operation for this run.

expiresAt.description: When the lease lapses and the run becomes claimable again. Renew before this.

epoch.description: The grant's epoch, minted server-side and monotonic. The runner writes it into the checkpoint it authors. A checkpoint whose epoch is above the current grant is refused (a row minted under a grant this holder never held) and one below the run's high-water epoch is refused as a rollback.

CheckpointWriteProblem.description: A refused checkpoint save. `type` says which refusal it is; `acceptedSequence` is present only when the refusal is a supersession, since a lease that is no longer current says nothing about which sequence the store would take.

acceptedSequence.description: The sequence the store will accept next, which is its persisted sequence plus one.

QuotaProblem.description: A quota rejection, naming the quota and the counter it was measured against so a runner can back off against the right dimension rather than globally.

quota.description: The quota that rejected the request.

counter.description: The counter the quota was measured against, for example the environment or tenant it applies to.

TimerClaimRequest.description: What the runner can execute, for a due-timer sweep. Neither the environment nor the due-time cutoff is a request parameter. The environment is resolved from the principal's bindings, and the cutoff is the server's own clock, because a runner naming a future cutoff would be asking to resume runs whose timers have not fired.

hostedVersions.description: The versioned workflow ids ({base}-v{n}) this runner has baked and can execute. A run for a version absent from this list is not offered, since claiming work the runner cannot execute would strand it until the lease expired.

limit.description: The most runs to claim in one call. The server bounds it. A sweep that claimed every matching run at once would hold a lease on each while the runner worked through them one at a time, so the bound is what keeps a large fan-out from being leased far longer than it is being executed.

leaseSeconds.description: The requested lease duration. The server bounds it; a request above the deployment's maximum is granted the maximum rather than refused.

MessageClaimRequest.description:
The channel a message arrived on, and what the runner can execute. The message payload is deliberately absent. The runner holds it and hands it to each resumed run itself, so delivering a message tells the control plane that one arrived on a channel, never what it said.

The correlation id is present because the wait it matches is already recorded server-side, so naming it discloses nothing the control plane does not hold, and omitting it widens the delivery to every run awaiting the channel.

channel.description: The channel the message arrived on.

correlationId.description: The delivered message's correlation token. A message carrying none matches every run awaiting the channel, whatever correlation each is waiting for, and a run awaiting the channel with no particular correlation is matched by any message on it. Otherwise the two must be equal. Absence is a wildcard on either side rather than a value in its own right.

hostedVersions.description: The versioned workflow ids ({base}-v{n}) this runner has baked and can execute. A run for a version absent from this list is not offered, since claiming work the runner cannot execute would strand it until the lease expired.

limit.description: The most runs to claim in one call. The server bounds it. A sweep that claimed every matching run at once would hold a lease on each while the runner worked through them one at a time, so the bound is what keeps a large fan-out from being leased far longer than it is being executed.

leaseSeconds.description: The requested lease duration. The server bounds it; a request above the deployment's maximum is granted the maximum rather than refused.

ClaimedRuns.description: The runs claimed by a sweep, each already leased to this runner. Unlike claiming a single run, an empty result is answered as an empty array rather than a 204. A sweep asks about a set, and an empty set has the same shape as a populated one, so the array already says 'none' without the client having to branch on the status code to learn it.

claims.description: The claimed runs, in no guaranteed order.

HostedVersion.description: A version this runner may execute, and the content hash its executor must match. The versioned workflow id a claim matches on is not carried: it is {base}-v{n}, so restating it would put derivable data on the wire and make the server compose a string per version on every poll.

baseWorkflowId.description: The unversioned identity the version belongs to.

versionNumber.description: The version number within the base workflow.

hash.description: The version's content hash, which the loaded executor is verified against.

HostedVersions.description: What this runner should be able to execute. The set is resolved from the principal's bindings and each environment's availability, so a runner is told what to host rather than reading the catalog and deciding for itself.

nextPageToken.description: Opaque continuation token; absent on the last page.
